d: The course’s unit of planned study time. One knowledge point is roughly one minute of focused study; the course totals 3,600.
An exam form used to evaluate new questions before an exam goes live. Some items may be revised or removed after analysis.
The process ISC2 uses to determine the tasks practitioners actually perform, so the exam tests what the role really involves.
The share of exam questions drawn from a domain. On this exam, Domain 1 is 10% and the others range from 17% to 19%.
A word such as BEST, MOST, FIRST or LEAST that determines which of several reasonable answers is correct.
Studying by recalling information from memory, for example with questions or flash cards, rather than rereading it.
Reviewing material at increasing intervals so it moves into long-term memory.
The testing centre network where the AI Security pilot exam is delivered.
The field of building machines that perform tasks normally requiring human intelligence, such as perception, reasoning, learning and language.
The part of AI in which systems learn patterns from data rather than following explicitly programmed rules.
Machine learning using neural networks with many layers, which learn their own features from data.
AI that creates new content such as text, images, audio, video or code.
AI that performs a specific task or range of tasks. All AI in production today is narrow AI.
Hypothetical AI matching human capability across most domains.
AI built from explicit, human-written rules and logic, such as expert systems.
A model that learns the boundary between classes in order to label inputs.
A model that learns the distribution of its data and can produce new samples from it.
A large model trained on broad data that can be adapted to many downstream tasks.
Learning from examples paired with correct labels, for classification or regression.
Learning structure from unlabelled data, for clustering, dimensionality reduction or anomaly detection.
Learning a policy of actions that maximises cumulative reward from an environment.
Learning from labels derived from the data itself, such as predicting the next word; used to pretrain foundation models.
Reinforcement learning from human feedback: tuning a model with a reward model trained on human preference rankings.
Training a shared model across many participants who send model updates instead of raw data.
Reusing a model trained for one task as the starting point for another.
A measurable property of an input that a model uses to make predictions.
The correct answer attached to a training example in supervised learning.
When a model fits its training data too closely and performs worse on new data.
The algorithm that computes how much each weight contributed to the error, by working backwards through the network.
The optimisation method that adjusts weights in small steps to reduce the loss.
A setting chosen before training, such as learning rate, batch size or number of layers.
One complete pass through the training data.
An evolutionary optimisation method using a population, a fitness function, selection, crossover and mutation.
A network that applies sliding filters to grid-like data such as images.
A network that processes sequences step by step, carrying a hidden state as memory.
Long short-term memory: an RNN design with gates that control what is remembered or forgotten.
A neural architecture based on self-attention that processes whole sequences in parallel; the basis of modern LLMs.
A mechanism that scores the relevance of every token to every other token and blends their information.
Graphics processing unit: a massively parallel processor used to train and serve neural networks.
Tensor processing unit: Google’s custom chip for neural-network arithmetic.
Neural processing unit: a low-power AI accelerator in phones, laptops and edge devices.
Reducing the numerical precision of model weights to save memory and speed up inference, at some cost in accuracy.
A knowledge base of adversary tactics, techniques and case studies targeting AI systems.
A ranked list of the most critical security risks in applications built on large language models.
The NIST AI Risk Management Framework, organised into the Govern, Map, Measure and Manage functions.
A single number measuring how wrong a model’s predictions are, which training tries to minimise.
A loss that is low when a model gives high probability to the correct answer; standard for classifiers and language models.
The size of each gradient descent step: too small and training is slow, too large and the loss oscillates or diverges.
An optimiser that adapts the step size for each weight using running averages of past gradients.
The raw scores a model’s final layer outputs, one per possible output, before softmax turns them into probabilities.
The function that converts logits into probabilities that sum to 1; dividing logits by a temperature first sharpens or flattens the result.
An architecture in which a router sends each token to a few of many expert sub-networks, so only part of the model runs for each token.
The small network in a mixture-of-experts layer that scores the experts and chooses which ones process each token.
In a mixture-of-experts model, the parameters actually used for a given token; compute follows them, but memory must hold every expert.
A transformer-based generative model of text with billions of parameters, trained on vast amounts of text and code.
A model that processes or produces more than one type of data, such as text, images and audio.
A generative model that creates images or video by progressively removing noise.
A generation setting controlling randomness: low values favour likely tokens, high values add variety.
Sampling only from the smallest set of tokens whose combined probability reaches a threshold p.
A model whose trained weights are published so it can be downloaded, self-hosted and modified.
The unit of text a model processes: a word, part of a word or a character, represented as a number.
A subword tokenisation method that merges frequent character pairs into tokens.
An NLP technique that finds and classifies entities such as names, organisations and identifiers.
Converting equivalent Unicode forms, such as full-width letters and ligatures, to a standard form so filters treat them consistently.
Look-alike letters from different alphabets, such as Cyrillic and Latin, mapped to a common form by Unicode Technical Standard #39 checks.
The maximum number of tokens, input plus output, that a model can process in one request.
The tendency of models to use information at the start and end of a long context more reliably than in the middle.
A vector of numbers representing the meaning of content, used for similarity search.
A measure of how closely two vectors point in the same direction.
A database that stores embeddings with their text and metadata and searches them by similarity.
Indexing methods that find similar vectors quickly at scale, trading a little accuracy for speed.
Reconstructing original text from embeddings, showing that vectors are sensitive data.
Designing model inputs so they reliably produce the desired output.
Developer instructions setting a model’s role, rules and boundaries.
Including worked examples in a prompt so the model infers the pattern.
Asking a model to reason through intermediate steps before answering.
Retrieving relevant content at request time and supplying it to the model to ground its answer.
Splitting documents into passages before embedding and indexing them.
Re-scoring retrieved candidates with a more precise model to keep the most relevant.
Malicious instructions delivered through content a model processes, such as documents, web pages or tool output.
Further training a pretrained model on task-specific data to adapt its behaviour.
Adapting a model by training a small number of new parameters while freezing the rest.
Low-rank adaptation: learning weight changes as the product of two small matrices added to frozen weights.
LoRA fine-tuning on top of a 4-bit quantised base model.
A system in which a model pursues a goal over multiple steps, planning and acting with tools.
A model outputting a structured request to use a tool, which the application decides whether to execute.
An open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data sources.
A protocol that lets AI agents discover each other’s capabilities and delegate tasks.
Information an agent retains: short-term in its context, long-term in external stores, or shared between agents.
Maintaining an agent’s state, memory and credentials across turns and sessions.
Granting an AI system more functionality, permissions or autonomy than its task requires.
Model output that is fluent and plausible but false, fabricated or unsupported by its sources.
NIST’s term, in the Generative AI Profile (AI 600-1), for confidently stated but erroneous or false content.
Output that contradicts the source material the model was given.
Output that adds claims the source material cannot support.
The degree to which an output’s claims are supported by its source or retrieved passages.
A system declining to answer, for example saying “I don’t know”, when it lacks reliable information.
Producing different outputs for the same input, due to sampling, hardware effects, updates or changing context.
Uncertainty from inherent noise or ambiguity in data; more data does not reduce it.
Uncertainty from gaps in a model’s knowledge; better or more data can reduce it.
How well a model’s confidence matches its actual accuracy.
The average gap between a model’s stated confidence and its observed accuracy.
An input unlike the data a model was trained on, where its predictions are least reliable.
Registering software package names that AI models hallucinate, so that developers install malicious code.
A change in the distribution of a model’s inputs compared with its training data.
A change in the relationship between inputs and outcomes, so learned patterns stop holding.
A change in the mix of outcomes, such as a rising fraud rate.
Declining model performance over time; the symptom of underlying drift.
A change in a generative AI system’s outputs caused by changes to its model, prompts, retrieval or tools.
A statistic that measures how much a variable’s distribution has shifted between two datasets.
A fixed set of representative and adversarial test cases, re-run after every change to detect regressions.
Fixing a dependency, such as a hosted model, to a specific version so that changes happen only when chosen.
Progressive loss of information about the real data distribution when models train on model-generated data.
Data generated by a model or simulation rather than collected from real-world events.
A table of true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives for a classifier.
TP ÷ (TP + FP): the proportion of positive predictions that are correct.
TP ÷ (TP + FN): the proportion of actual positives that are detected.
The harmonic mean of precision and recall.
FP ÷ (FP + TN): the proportion of actual negatives wrongly flagged.
High accuracy that hides poor detection, typical when the event of interest is rare.
A plot of true positive rate against false positive rate across thresholds; AUC summarises it from 0.5 (chance) to 1.0.
The score above which a classifier’s output is treated as positive.
Automatic metrics that score generated text by its word overlap with reference text.
The probability that at least one of k generated code samples passes the unit tests.
A measure of how well a model predicts text; lower means better prediction.
Using a language model to score or compare other models’ outputs against a rubric.
Benchmark test items appearing in training data, inflating scores.
When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.
The proportion of adversarial attempts against a system that achieve their goal.
An operational mode in which a person approves each AI decision before it takes effect.
An operational mode in which the AI acts while people monitor it and can intervene or override.
The tendency to over-rely on automated recommendations, even when they are wrong.
Running a model on live cases without letting it act, to compare its decisions with human ones.
The system of decision rights, roles, policies and controls that keeps AI use aligned with objectives, values and legal obligations.
Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, a risk-based law setting obligations for AI systems and general-purpose AI models used in the EU.
An AI use banned under Article 5 of the EU AI Act, such as social scoring or untargeted facial scraping.
Under the AI Act, a safety component of a regulated product or a system used in a sensitive area listed in Annex III.
A model trained on broad data that can perform a wide range of tasks and be integrated into many systems.
Under the AI Act, an organisation using an AI system under its authority in a professional capacity.
The process of demonstrating that a high-risk AI system meets the AI Act’s requirements.
An assessment certain deployers must complete before using high-risk AI, covering impacts on people’s rights.
Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, which amended the AI Act, delaying high-risk deadlines and adjusting some duties.
A GDPR assessment required before processing likely to result in high risk to individuals.
The right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects, subject to exceptions and safeguards.
The international standard specifying requirements for an AI management system; certifiable.
The policies, processes, roles and controls an organisation uses to govern AI, as defined in ISO/IEC 42001.
A document listing which reference controls apply, which don’t, and why.
Guidance on AI risk management, based on ISO 31000.
The NIST Generative AI Profile, describing twelve risks that generative AI creates or worsens.
A mapping between frameworks, showing how controls in one satisfy requirements in another.
A record of legal and contractual requirements mapped to controls and owners.
A mandatory, high-level statement of management intent and direction.
A mandatory, specific requirement that makes a policy measurable.
Step-by-step instructions for performing a task consistently.
Recommended, non-mandatory good practice.
A centralised, maintained record of all AI systems and use cases with owners, tiers, controls and status.
An executive accountable for AI strategy, governance and coordination.
A cross-functional body with authority to approve, condition or reject AI use cases.
A role that champions responsible AI principles and leads ethical reviews.
A trained advocate embedded in a business team who promotes safe AI adoption.
A governance model separating risk ownership (first line), oversight (second line) and independent assurance (third line).
Designing, building and using AI in line with principles such as fairness, safety, privacy, inclusiveness, transparency and accountability.
Ensuring AI works well for people of different abilities, languages, cultures and circumstances.
Presenting an appearance of ethical AI without operational substance, owners or effect on decisions.
Intergovernmental principles for trustworthy AI, adopted in 2019 and updated in 2024.

t: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI
d: A 2021 global standard on AI ethics adopted by all UNESCO member states.
A personal attribute, such as race, sex, age or disability, on which discrimination is prohibited by law.
A neutral-seeming practice or model that disproportionately disadvantages a protected group without adequate justification.
Treating someone less favourably because of a protected characteristic.
A feature that correlates with a protected characteristic and can reproduce its effects.
Bias that exists in the world and is captured in data even when the data is collected accurately.
Bias caused by under- or over-sampling of certain groups in data.
Bias caused by flawed labels or proxies, such as using cost as a proxy for health need.
A fairness criterion requiring equal selection rates across groups.
A fairness criterion requiring equal true positive rates across groups.
A fairness criterion requiring equal true positive and false positive rates across groups.
A fairness criterion requiring equal precision across groups.
A group’s selection rate divided by the highest group’s rate; below 0.8 suggests potential adverse impact.
The ability to give human-understandable reasons for an AI system’s outputs.
The degree to which a human can understand how a model works internally.
Shapley additive explanations: a method that attributes a prediction to each input feature using game theory.
Local interpretable model-agnostic explanations: approximates a model locally with a simple surrogate.
An explanation describing the smallest input change that would alter the outcome.
A document summarising a model’s purpose, training data, performance across groups and limitations.
An effect that emerges from widespread or interconnected AI use rather than from one system.
Correlated failure arising when many organisations depend on the same model or provider.
Total data centre energy divided by the energy used by IT equipment; closer to 1.0 is more efficient.
Risk before any controls are considered.
Risk remaining after controls; never zero.
The amount and type of risk an organisation is willing to pursue or retain in pursuit of its objectives.
The acceptable variation around objectives, often expressed as thresholds for specific risks.
A metric that signals rising risk exposure, such as drift scores or blocked injection attempts.
The percentage of an asset’s value lost in a single loss event.
Asset value × exposure factor: the expected cost of one occurrence.
The expected number of occurrences per year.
SLE × ARO: the expected loss per year from a risk scenario.
ALE before the control − ALE after − the control’s annual cost.
Factor Analysis of Information Risk: a quantitative model based on loss event frequency and loss magnitude.
A chart plotting risks by likelihood and impact to show priorities.
A one-sentence description of a risk’s cause, event and consequence.
An assessment of an AI system’s consequences for individuals, groups and society (ISO/IEC 42001, 42005).
A public-sector assessment that scores an automated system’s impact and sets required safeguards.
The extent of damage a system could cause if it fails or is compromised, set by its data, action and connection reach.
A category that sets the depth of assessment, oversight and approval a use case needs.
Matching the effort spent on assessment and control to the size of the risk.
Not starting or continuing an activity, or removing the source of risk.
Applying controls that reduce likelihood or impact.
Sharing financial consequences with another party, such as an insurer; accountability is not transferred.
A documented, time-bound decision by an authorised owner to retain a risk within appetite.
An event, defined in advance, that requires an AI risk or impact assessment to be revisited.
Information relating to an identified or identifiable person, including indirect identifiers.
GDPR Article 9 data, such as health, biometric, ethnic origin, religious and sexual orientation data, with stricter rules.
Individually identifiable health information held by HIPAA covered entities and business associates.
A HIPAA contract requiring vendors that handle PHI to safeguard it.
Payment card data, such as the primary account number, protected under PCI DSS.
Technical data whose transfer to certain countries or foreign persons is restricted by export laws.
Deriving sensitive attributes about a person from other data or model outputs.
A model storing and reproducing specific training examples.
Identifying individuals in supposedly anonymous data by combining it with other information.
Regulated data entering AI pipelines so that its legal obligations attach to models, indexes and outputs.
A US copyright defence assessed case by case on purpose, nature, amount and market effect.
EU copyright exceptions permitting automated analysis, with a commercial exception that rightsholders can opt out of.
A rightsholder’s machine-readable statement that content may not be used for text and data mining.
The public summary of training data that GPAI providers must publish under the EU AI Act.
The US requirement that a work have a human author to be protected by copyright.
A vendor’s contractual promise to defend customers against IP claims, usually with conditions.
The principle that personal data is kept no longer than necessary.
An instruction to preserve relevant data for litigation or investigation, suspending deletion.
Rendering encrypted data unrecoverable by destroying its keys.
A provider option under which prompts and outputs are not stored beyond processing.
A GDPR lawful basis requiring a documented balancing test and offering a right to object.
Automated collection of data from websites; still subject to privacy law, terms and copyright.
Assessing an AI provider’s data handling, security, model governance, assurance, resilience and legal terms before and during use.
The Cloud Security Alliance’s vendor-neutral framework of AI security and governance control objectives.
CSA’s assurance programme for AI providers, with self-assessment and third-party certification levels.
Contractual commitments on availability, support, vulnerability remediation and related security performance.
Contract terms requiring a vendor to report incidents within a defined time, with details and cooperation.
A contractual commitment to warn customers before model versions change, often with version pinning.
A third party engaged by a vendor that processes the customer’s data.
Arrangements for data return, deletion certification and transition when a vendor relationship ends.
The EU directive on cybersecurity for essential and important entities, including 24-hour early warning of significant incidents.
The EU Digital Operational Resilience Act for financial entities, including ICT third-party risk requirements.
A machine-readable inventory of software components, versions, suppliers and licences.
An inventory of an AI system’s models, datasets, adapters, software, services and their provenance and licences.
The CycloneDX format’s support for machine-learning bills of materials.
SPDX extensions for describing AI models and datasets.
The division of security duties between a service provider and its customer, which varies by service type.
Hardware-isolated execution that protects code and data from the host, hypervisor and operator.
Protecting data in use by processing it inside an attested, hardware-based TEE.
Hardware-signed evidence of the code and configuration running in a TEE, verified before trust is granted.
Releasing secrets, such as model keys, only to environments whose attestation satisfies policy.
Extracting secrets by observing indirect effects such as timing, power or cache behaviour.
The right to pause, adjust or redirect a running AI process.
The right to replace an AI output with a human decision in an individual case.
The right to give formal approval at lifecycle gates, such as deployment or risk acceptance.
The right to halt an AI system entirely, backed by a tested kill switch.
A table showing who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed for each activity.
The defined route by which concerns move to people with greater authority.
AI tools, models or features used without the organisation’s knowledge, approval or governance.
A control point that discovers and governs use of cloud services, including AI tools.
Controls that detect and block sensitive data leaving approved boundaries.
A period in which teams can register unsanctioned tools without penalty.
Documentation of a deployed AI system, its components, safeguards and oversight.
Documentation of a dataset’s provenance, composition, collection and appropriate uses.
A record of significant decisions, including who decided, when, on what evidence and why.
A documented, approved, time-limited departure from policy with compensating controls.
Transparency duties for AI interaction, synthetic content marking, deepfakes and certain AI-generated text.
Embedding a detectable signal in content to indicate it was AI-generated.
Signed provenance metadata describing how content was created and edited.
An independent internal function giving the board assurance over governance, risk and controls.
An audit by an independent third party, for certification, legal or assurance purposes.
An independent assessment of an AI system’s outcomes across demographic groups.
Ongoing, often automated, testing of controls using monitoring data between periodic audits.
The skills, knowledge and understanding people need to use and oversee AI appropriately; supported under Article 4 of the EU AI Act.
A structured description of the skills and levels required for each role.
Comparing current skills with required competencies to find and prioritise shortfalls.
Training tailored to the responsibilities and risks of a specific role.
Brief guidance delivered at the moment it is needed, such as a prompt inside an AI tool.
A four-level training evaluation model: reaction, learning, behaviour and results.
A metric that predicts future risk or performance.
A metric that records outcomes after the fact.
A culture in which people recognise, discuss and report risk openly and act on it.
Confidence that one can report mistakes or concerns without blame or punishment.
An event that could have caused harm but didn’t, valuable for learning when reported.
The person accountable for a dataset’s classification, permitted uses and access.
The person responsible for day-to-day data quality, metadata and standards.
The person or team that operates storage and technical controls for data on the owner’s behalf.
Under GDPR, the party that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data.
Under GDPR, a party that processes personal data on a controller’s behalf and instructions.
The GDPR Article 28 contract between controller and processor.
The principle that data is subject to the laws of the jurisdiction where it is located or controlled.
The geographic location where data is stored and processed.
A legal requirement that certain data remain within national borders.
Approved contract terms used to legitimise transfers of personal data outside the EEA.
Assigning sensitivity levels to data based on the impact of compromise.
Carrying classification and handling metadata through transformations such as chunking and embedding.
An assessment of purpose fit, derivation risks and safeguards before sensitive data is used for AI.
Combining individually harmless data to reveal sensitive information.
A record of data’s origin, collection method, rights and history.
A record of how data flows and is transformed into datasets, models and outputs.
A tamper-evident record of who held, accessed or transferred data, and when.
Giving each dataset snapshot an immutable identifier, often a content hash.
Extending deletion from source records to every derived copy and artefact.
Building privacy into systems from the outset, following seven foundational principles such as proactive protection and privacy as the default.

t: Data protection by design and by default
d: The GDPR Article 25 duty to build in privacy measures at design time and, by default, process only the personal data each purpose needs.
Collecting personal data for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes, and not reusing it in incompatible ways.
Processing only personal data that is adequate, relevant and limited to what the purpose needs.
One of the six GDPR grounds, such as consent, contract or legitimate interests, that make processing lawful.
Hiding all or part of a value, either in a permanent copy (static masking) or at display time (dynamic masking).
Replacing a sensitive value with a surrogate token, with the original held in a secure vault for authorised recovery.
A hash computed with a secret key, so predictable inputs can’t be recovered by hashing every possible value.
Replacing identifiers so data can’t be linked to a person without separately held additional information. The result is still personal data.
Processing data so that people can no longer be identified by any means reasonably likely to be used. Anonymous data is outside the GDPR.
An attribute, such as postcode, birth date or sex, that can identify people when combined with others.
A property where each record is indistinguishable from at least k−1 others on its quasi-identifiers.
Extensions of k-anonymity that also protect the sensitive values within each group of records.
The UK ICO test of whether a competent person without specialist skills could re-identify individuals from data.
A mathematical guarantee that an output reveals very little about whether any one person’s data was included.
The parameter that bounds privacy loss in differential privacy. Smaller ε means more noise and stronger privacy; spending accumulates.
Differential privacy applied on the user’s device before data is collected, so the collector never sees true values.
Differentially private stochastic gradient descent: training with per-example gradient clipping and calibrated noise.
Adding random perturbation to data or results to obscure individual values; without calibration it offers no formal guarantee.
De-identification by removing 18 types of identifier, with no actual knowledge that the remaining data could identify someone.
De-identification where a qualified expert documents that the risk of re-identification is very small.
The HIPAA rule limiting uses and disclosures of PHI to the minimum needed for the purpose.
Card security codes, full track data and PINs, which PCI DSS forbids storing after authorisation.
Determining whether a specific person’s data was included in a model’s training set.
Deducing sensitive characteristics about a person from a model’s outputs or from ordinary data about them.
Unequal outcomes driven by features, such as postcode, that correlate with a protected characteristic.
Techniques for removing the influence of specific training data from a model without full retraining.
Sharded, isolated, sliced and aggregated training, which lets erasure requests be met by retraining only one shard.
The most that one person’s data can change a query’s answer; the noise needed scales with it.
Adds noise drawn from a Laplace distribution with scale sensitivity ÷ ε, giving pure ε-differential privacy.
Adds normally distributed noise scaled to the L2 sensitivity, giving (ε, δ)-differential privacy; used in DP-SGD.
In (ε, δ)-differential privacy, the small probability that the ε bound fails; it should be far below one divided by the number of people.
The rule that privacy loss adds up across releases computed from the same data.
The rule that releases computed on disjoint groups of people cost only the largest ε.
The property that anything computed from a differentially private output stays private, at no extra cost.
A method or tool that tracks the total privacy loss across queries or training steps, such as a Rényi DP accountant.
What one protected unit is in a differential privacy guarantee: a record, a user or a device.
The accuracy, completeness and freedom from unauthorised change of data used to train models.
Ensuring no single person can both make and approve a change, such as editing training data and releasing it for training.
A cryptographic fingerprint of data; any change to the content produces a different hash.
A digitally signed list of a dataset’s files, hashes and lineage, verified before the data is used.
Write-once storage in which approved data can’t be modified or deleted for a set period.
Evaluation data appearing in training data, which inflates measured performance.
Deliberately manipulating training data to change a model’s behaviour.
Poisoning aimed at degrading a model’s overall performance.
Poisoning aimed at causing errors on specific, chosen inputs while overall performance looks normal.
Hidden model behaviour that activates only when a specific trigger appears in the input.
Poisoning with correctly labelled but subtly manipulated samples, which defeats label review.
Poisoning a dataset distributed as URLs by changing the content behind those URLs after the dataset is defined.
Recovering memorised training content from a model through its outputs.
A unique, random string planted in training data to measure whether a model memorises and reproduces it.
Reconstructing features or representative examples of training data from a model.
Changing the labels on training examples, randomly or to cause specific behaviour.
Items with known correct labels mixed into annotation work to measure annotator accuracy.
A measure of how consistently different annotators label the same items.
File formats, such as Python pickle, that can execute code when loaded.
Training models on data generated by earlier models, which creates feedback loops.
The transfer of hidden traits from a teacher model to a student through data with no obvious link to those traits.
How closely synthetic data preserves the statistical properties and rare cases of real data.
Tools and processes that discover and classify data stores, map access and remediate exposure, continuously.
Tools that check cloud infrastructure configuration against security benchmarks.
Tools that inventory AI models, endpoints and services and check their configuration.
Unmanaged or forgotten copies of data outside approved, governed stores.
Detecting sensitive or unsafe content by meaning, using classifiers, embeddings or language models.
A proxy in front of model APIs that applies policy, inspection, routing and logging to AI traffic.
Detecting copies of known sensitive records or documents by comparing fingerprints or hashes.
Replacing sensitive values with tokens before an external model, and restoring them in the response.
Protecting data while it is processed, for example in trusted execution environments.
TLS in which both client and server authenticate with certificates.
Encrypting data with a data key, which is itself encrypted by a key-encryption key held in a KMS or HSM.
Tamper-resistant hardware that generates, stores and uses cryptographic keys.
A service that stores keys and controls and logs their use, often backed by HSMs.
A key held in a provider’s KMS but governed by the customer’s policy, rotation and audit.
Generating keys yourself and importing them into a provider’s key management service.
Keeping keys in the customer’s own system, so the provider must request each use.
The time span during which a specific key is authorised for use.
Short-lived credentials issued to software based on its verified identity, instead of static keys.
Collecting encrypted data today in the hope of decrypting it with future quantum computers.
Granting access based on the declared and approved purpose of a request.
Granting access based on attributes of the user, resource, action and context.
A governed inventory of data products with owners, tags, lineage and approved uses.
Hiding sensitive values at query time according to who is asking and why.
The three levels of media sanitisation, protecting against simple recovery, laboratory recovery and any reuse.
Sanitising media by destroying the keys that encrypt all data on it.
Destroying dense media into very small particles so no fragment holds recoverable data.
A record documenting how, when and by whom media was sanitised and verified.
The named person, usually in the business, accountable for a model’s use and outcomes.
A discipline, long required of banks, for governing models through sound development, independent validation and oversight.
Critical review of a model by objective, informed people with the authority to make change happen.
Testing and review of a model by people who didn’t build it, before approval and periodically afterwards.
The evidence, approvers, conditions and review cycle a model must pass through for its risk tier.
The authoritative record of model versions, with their status, lineage, evidence, approvals and deployments.
An automated check that allows only approved, verified model versions to be deployed.
A model weight format that stores tensors only, so loading it can’t execute embedded code.
Signed metadata describing how an artefact was built: its source, inputs, environment and process.
Passing model output to other components without validation or encoding (OWASP LLM05).
Escaping output for where it will be used, such as HTML, SQL or a shell, so it can’t run as code.
Rebuilding files without active or hidden content, such as macros, scripts, hidden text and metadata.
Releasing a new version to a small share of users first, and widening it only if monitoring stays healthy.
Running two production environments and switching traffic between them, so rollback is immediate.
Everything needed to restore a previous version: model, prompts, settings, guardrails, index and serving stack.
A pre-built way to disable an AI feature quickly and fall back to a non-AI process.
The metrics, thresholds, review frequency and owner set at approval for watching a model in production.
The largest acceptable gap in a fairness metric between groups, set at approval and monitored.
A provider’s system for collecting and reviewing data on a high-risk AI system’s performance after release (EU AI Act, Article 72).
A recordable action involving AI data, such as dataset access, training, deployment, inference or erasure.
A log whose entries can’t be altered or removed without detection, for example through hash chaining.
A sequence of records in which each includes the hash of the one before, so any change breaks the chain.
Exceptional access that requires approval and a stated purpose, and is fully logged.
The learned parameters of a trained model; together with the architecture, they are the model.
Confidential business information protected by law, provided reasonable measures are taken to keep it secret.
A control requiring two authorised people to approve or carry out a sensitive action, such as exporting weights.
Disclosure of a system prompt’s contents through the model’s responses (OWASP LLM07).
Recreating a model’s functionality or parameters by querying it and training on its answers.
Training a smaller model to imitate a larger model’s outputs; used without permission, a form of extraction.
A model trained on a target model’s answers to imitate its behaviour.
Returning only the detail a use case needs, such as a label instead of full probability scores.
Likelihood scores for output tokens that some LLM APIs return; useful to developers and to extraction attackers.
A hidden, verifiable signal embedded in a model to prove ownership.
Secret inputs trained to produce specific outputs, used to test whether a suspect model was copied.
A signal embedded in generated content so that it can be identified as coming from a model.
A characteristic that identifies a model or a specific copy of it, whether observed or embedded.
A unique mark embedded in each distributed copy of a model, so a leak can be traced to its source.
A fixed-length digest of data; any change to the data produces a different digest.
Cryptographic proof, made with a private key, that data is unchanged and came from the signer.
A list of every file in a model package with its digest, which is then signed.
Signing with short-lived certificates tied to a verified identity and recorded in a transparency log, as in Sigstore.
A Python serialisation format that can run code when loaded, which makes untrusted model files dangerous.
Uncontrolled use of an AI service that leads to denial of service, cost exhaustion or model theft (OWASP LLM10).
An attack that drives up usage costs on a pay-per-use service until budgets are exhausted.
A cap on requests or tokens per identity over a short time window.
An allowance of calls or tokens per user, team or application over a longer period.
A spending limit that raises alerts and then stops or degrades usage.
A rate-limiting algorithm that allows short bursts while enforcing an average rate.
A mechanism that stops calls to a failing dependency, then retries it gradually.
Reducing service step by step during a failure, instead of failing completely.
Blocking or holding activity when a security control is unavailable, rather than bypassing the control.
The external data, models, software, services and infrastructure an AI system depends on.
Making malicious edits to a source just before a scheduled snapshot captures it.
An organisation’s own verified copy of external data or artefacts, used instead of live downloads.
Referring to an artefact by the hash of its content, so any change is detected and rejected.
Where an artefact came from and how it was made, supported by records such as attestations and AIBOMs.
Assurance that an artefact really comes from its claimed source and hasn’t been altered.
Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts: a framework of assurance levels for how artefacts are built and how their provenance is recorded.
An account on a hub or registry whose identity the platform has confirmed.
Publishing malicious packages or models under names that imitate popular ones.
Re-registering a deleted or transferred publisher name on a model hub, so name-based references pull an impostor.
Tricking an installer into fetching a malicious public package instead of a private one with the same name.
Loader options that run code shipped with a model or dataset; disable them for untrusted sources.
A model trained to behave normally until a trigger appears; research showed such behaviour can persist through safety training.
The weakening of a model’s safety behaviour through further fine-tuning, even on benign data.
Under the EU AI Act, a general-purpose AI model with high-impact capabilities and extra duties such as adversarial testing and incident reporting.
Many organisations depending on the same few models or providers, so one failure spreads widely.
A weakness in a base model, such as a working jailbreak, that carries over to models built on it.
A security model with no implicit trust from network location: every request is authenticated, authorised and checked against policy (NIST SP 800-207).
The component that allows or blocks a request according to a policy decision.
Dividing networks and workloads into small zones with tightly controlled traffic between them.
Layered, independent controls, so that the failure of one doesn’t lead to compromise.
Safe out of the box, without users having to configure extra protection.
CISA-led principles asking vendors to own customer security outcomes, be transparent, and lead from the top.
A point where data or control passes between components with different levels of trust.
A diagram of components, data stores, external entities and data flows, used as the basis of a threat model.
A threat categorisation: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege.
A threat modelling framework for agentic AI systems from the Cloud Security Alliance.
Filtering retrieved content by the requesting user’s permissions before it reaches the model.
A short record of a significant design decision: context, options, consequences and accepted risk.
Applying cheap checks to every request and expensive checks only where risk is high.
The maximum response time a use case can tolerate, shared among all processing steps.
All costs of an option over its life, including infrastructure, staff, tooling and compliance.
Under the EU AI Act, a change to an AI system that affects its compliance or intended purpose, which can make the modifier its provider.
In the Model Context Protocol, the AI application (host) runs clients that connect to servers exposing tools, resources and prompts.
Hidden instructions in a tool’s description or metadata that manipulate how a model behaves.
A tool whose definition or behaviour changes after it has been reviewed and approved.
One tool server’s descriptions influencing how a model uses another server’s tools.
Accepting a token issued for one service and forwarding it to another; forbidden by the MCP specification.
A component tricked into using its own authority on behalf of a party that shouldn’t have it.
In the Agent2Agent protocol, a published description of an agent’s capabilities, endpoint and authentication requirements.
Checking that the caller may access the specific record requested, not just the API; its absence is a top API weakness.
A 2024 campaign that exploited internet-exposed, unauthenticated Ray clusters to steal credentials, data and compute.
Consensus hardening guides for operating systems, cloud platforms, Kubernetes and applications.
Cloud-wide preventive rules, such as service control policies, that block risky configurations like public buckets.
Defining infrastructure in version-controlled code, so it can be reviewed, tested and checked against policy.
An out-of-band management processor on servers; its interface must be isolated and patched.
Kubernetes profiles (privileged, baseline and restricted) that limit what workloads may do.
A lightweight virtual machine that gives strong isolation with fast start-up, often used for sandboxes.
A container runtime that adds a user-space kernel or virtual machine layer for stronger isolation.
An isolated environment for sensitive training, with controlled access, no internet egress and controlled export.
Inferring other users’ prompts from response timing when caches are shared between users.
Physical and logical separation with no network path to other systems.
Deciding whether, and at what priority, new work may enter a system.
Dropping or deferring low-priority work under pressure to protect critical services.
Stopping lower-priority workloads so that higher-priority ones can run.
A cap on the resources a team, namespace or tenant may consume.
Using hijacked computing resources to mine cryptocurrency.
Workloads taking turns on a whole GPU and sharing its memory, which gives weak isolation.
Hardware partitioning of a GPU into instances with dedicated memory, cache and compute.
A 2024 GPU vulnerability that let one process read data left in local memory by another.
Compute committed in advance for a workload, so it isn’t lost to shortages or reclaim.
N+1 adds one spare component; 2N fully duplicates systems and paths.
Cooling that pipes liquid to cold plates mounted on processors.
Submerging hardware in dielectric fluid to remove heat.
An entry vestibule with two interlocked doors that admits one person at a time.
Detection that continuously samples air through pipes, giving very early warning of fire.
A sprinkler system whose pipes stay dry until two independent signals occur.
Ratings from Tier I (basic capacity) to Tier IV (fault tolerant) for data centre infrastructure.
Running untrusted code inside a CI/CD pipeline so that it gains the pipeline’s privileges.
OWASP’s list of the main risks to CI/CD systems, such as weak flow control and poor credential hygiene.
A build machine created fresh for each job and destroyed afterwards.
Exchanging a workload’s verified identity for short-lived cloud credentials, replacing stored keys.
Builds on a hardened platform that isolates builds from each other, so provenance can’t be forged.
A container image containing only an application and its runtime dependencies, without a shell or package manager.
A container build that compiles in one stage and copies only the results into a minimal final image.
A Kubernetes component that checks resources, such as image signatures, before the cluster accepts them.
Data layers called bronze (raw), silver (cleaned) and gold (curated).
Where new data is held until it passes validation and scanning.
An agreement between producer and consumer on a data feed’s schema, quality, meaning and ownership.
An open standard for collecting lineage metadata from data jobs.
Combining the weights of two or more models into one.
Signed evidence of a pipeline gate’s checks and result, bound to an artefact’s digest.
Rules written in machine-readable form and enforced automatically, for example by Open Policy Agent.
A hard gate blocks on failure; a soft gate warns and requires acknowledgement.
Adjusting a trained model so it forgets specific data without full retraining; it needs verification.
Retraining only the sub-model trained on the shard that held the data to forget, as in SISA.
A list of data to remove that feeds each scheduled retraining or index rebuild.
A benchmark that tests whether a model can forget facts about fictitious authors.
Supposedly forgotten knowledge reappearing after a small amount of further training.
A control around a model that checks or constrains its inputs, context, outputs or actions.
Keeping instructions and untrusted content in separate, labelled parts of the context, and checking content before it is added.
Delimiting, marking or encoding untrusted content so the model treats it as data rather than instructions.
Training a model to give system and developer instructions priority over user input, and user input over tool content.
Reserving space for system and safety instructions, and truncating untrusted content first.
The categories, severity levels and actions (block, warn, escalate) that content filters enforce.
The code that runs an agent’s loop: it calls the model, checks and executes proposed actions, and decides when to stop.
An agent pattern in which the full plan is produced and checked before any tool runs.
A pattern in which a planner never sees untrusted content, and a separate model reads it but can’t act.
A rule that ends an agent run, such as a budget limit, loop detection or a kill switch.
A versioned collection of test inputs with expected behaviour or reference answers.
The share of repeated runs in which a test case meets its criteria, used because AI outputs vary.
How long a user waits before a streamed response starts to appear.
Response times at high percentiles, such as p95 or p99, which show the slowest experiences.
A test of behaviour at expected traffic volumes, with realistic request mixes and sizes.
A test of behaviour under a sudden surge of traffic.
A test of sustained load over hours or days, to reveal leaks and slow degradation.
Increasing load until the system fails, to find its limit and how it fails.
Deliberately injecting failures to test a hypothesis about how a system behaves.
A planned exercise in which teams rehearse responding to injected failures.
Feeding random or structured variations of input to find crashes and unsafe behaviour.
Waiting progressively longer between retries, usually with random jitter, before giving up.
An action that has the same effect whether it is performed once or repeated.
An identity used by software rather than a person, such as a workload, service account, agent or tool.
A distinct identity for each AI agent, linked to a human sponsor and to the users it acts for.
The person accountable for an agent’s purpose, permissions and retirement.
Assurance that an actor can’t credibly deny an action, through identity binding, integrity, reliable time and protected evidence.
An agent acting for a user with a token that records both identities and only the scopes the task needs.
Acting with another identity’s credentials or session, so actions can’t be told apart from theirs.
An OAuth flow (RFC 8693) that swaps a token for a new one, for example recording an agent as the actor for a user.
A token bound to a key held by the client (for example DPoP or mTLS-bound), so a stolen copy can’t be replayed.
Digital signatures over HTTP requests (RFC 9421) that prove which key sent them and that they weren’t altered.
An OAuth flow in which a machine client authenticates itself to obtain an access token.
Client authentication by signing a short token with a private key, instead of sending a shared secret.
An open standard for issuing short-lived, attested identities (SVIDs) to workloads.
The service a token is intended for; APIs must reject tokens issued for other audiences.
The system that authenticates users and issues assertions or tokens to applications.
An XML-based federation standard widely used for enterprise web single sign-on.
An identity layer on OAuth 2.0 that issues ID tokens for authentication.
A standard API for provisioning and deprovisioning user accounts and groups in applications.
Authentication, such as FIDO2 passkeys or smart cards, that can’t be relayed through a fake site.
A FIDO2 credential stored on a device or synced, bound to the genuine site and unlocked locally.
An attack that floods a user with push approval requests until one is accepted.
Policies that grant, limit or block access based on signals such as device, location and risk.
Requiring fresh, stronger authentication before a sensitive action.
A central, audited store that issues and protects credentials, often backed by HSMs.
A credential generated on demand for one task or session, and revoked when it ends.
A tool layer attaching credentials to outbound calls, so an agent or model never handles them.
Automated detection of credentials in code, notebooks, logs, prompts and datasets.
Giving every identity, human or machine, only the access its current task needs.
Permissions that let one identity complete a sensitive process alone, such as creating and paying a supplier.
Splitting a sensitive action between one party who prepares it and another who approves it.
A purpose-built tool function with limited actions and arguments, instead of a generic capability.
Holding no permanent administrative rights, with access granted just in time for a task.
Temporary, approved, scoped elevation that is recorded and revoked automatically.
Tools and processes that control, record and broker privileged access.
The engine that evaluates a request against policy and returns a decision.
A condition attached to an allow decision, such as masking fields or requiring approval.
Re-evaluating access as context changes during a session, not only at sign-in.
A limit on what a component can run or reach, such as a sandbox, allow-list or egress rule.
Restricting outbound network connections to approved destinations.
A named permission in a token that limits which actions it allows.
A parameter (RFC 8707) that binds a token to a specific API audience.
An OAuth extension (RFC 9396) for fine-grained, transaction-level permissions, such as one specific payment.
Refusing anything not explicitly allowed.
Tools that offer more operations than a task needs (OWASP LLM06).
Tools or agents running with broader rights than a task needs (OWASP LLM06).
High-impact actions taken without independent verification or approval (OWASP LLM06).
Passing more authority to another agent or service than its task needs.
Narrowing authority at each delegation hop, so it can only shrink down a chain.
Using access to one system or agent to reach others.
Checking authorisation on every access in downstream systems, not just once at the start.
A continuously updated record of every human and non-human identity, with owner, purpose, credentials, permissions and activity.
An identity with no current, accountable owner.
An identity that hasn’t been used for a long period, such as 90 days.
The rights an identity actually holds once direct, group and inherited assignments are combined.
Standard access granted automatically to everyone in a given role.
The lifecycle events that should trigger provisioning, changes and removal of access.
A standard within the OpenID Shared Signals Framework that lets an identity provider tell applications to end sessions immediately.
Stopping access immediately but reversibly, then deleting once ownership, investigations and retention allow.
A periodic check by owners that each identity’s access is still needed and appropriate.
A small, event-triggered access review, such as after a role change or a new agent scope.
Continuous assessment of identity configuration, privilege, hygiene and secrets.
Tools that calculate effective and unused cloud permissions.
Detecting and responding to attacks on identities, such as token theft, in real time.
Metering and attributing AI token use and cost to identities, teams, agents and projects.
Reporting AI costs to the teams that incur them, with or without billing them internally.
Ending a session after a period of inactivity.
The maximum length of a session before re-authentication, however active the user is.
A maximum duration, number of steps or cost for a single agent task.
A pre-agreed route for urgent changes: a minimal logged request, pre-authorised approvers, deployment through the pipeline, and a review afterwards.
A record of who may perform each sensitive operation, and which combinations of duties one person or identity must not hold.
A check, soon after a change, that it was correct, complete and properly recorded.
The person responsible for a model’s day-to-day health: performance, monitoring, fixes and retraining.
The person who coordinates the response to an AI incident across teams, and owns its timeline and decision log.
Agreed authority over specific decisions, such as who may stop, restrict or roll back an AI system.
A containment step that on-call staff may take without further approval, such as switching to a fallback or disabling an agent.
A check before release that evaluation, security, monitoring, operations, resilience, thresholds and approval are all in place.
The share of AI outputs or recommendations that human reviewers reject or change.
The normal override rate, measured during pilots and early operation, used to set upper and lower alert thresholds.
Approving AI outputs without meaningful review, often as a result of automation bias.
An agreed band for guardrail blocks, refusals or validation failures, with defined actions when the rate goes above or below it.
The share of requests a model declines to answer, tracked as a signal of both over-restriction and eroded safety behaviour.
A guide for handling a type of incident: triggers, roles, decision points, containment options and communications.
Tested, step-by-step instructions for carrying out one operational task, such as rolling back a model.
A discussion-based walk-through of an incident scenario, used to test plans and roles without touching production.
New information introduced during an exercise to force participants to make decisions.
An exercise in which participants carry out real procedures in a test environment.
Any component whose settings are controlled, such as a model version, system prompt, guardrail policy, index or tool permission.
The approved, recorded state of a system’s configuration items, against which changes and drift are measured.
Holding configuration in version control, and applying it only through automated pipelines.
Any difference between the approved configuration baseline and what is actually running.
Automatically comparing a running system with the desired state in version control, and restoring or flagging differences.
A fixed set of test prompts run on a schedule to detect unannounced changes in a model’s behaviour.
The output of a training or retraining run, which must pass evaluation gates and approval before release.
Data about the operation of AI systems: prompts, outputs, retrieval, tool calls, API traffic and guardrail decisions, with their metadata.
An identifier carried by every event in one request, so its steps across the gateway, agent, retrieval, model and tools can be joined.
An open standard and toolkit for traces, metrics and logs, including semantic conventions for generative AI.
A platform that collects, normalises and correlates security events, and raises alerts.
A platform that runs playbooks to enrich alerts and automate response actions.
Adding context to events, such as identity, asset, model version and data classification.
A detection that fires when events occur in a set order within a time window or trace.
Baselining the behaviour of users, agents, keys and devices, and alerting on deviations.
A vendor-neutral schema for normalising security events from different sources.
Structured Threat Information Expression: a standard language for describing threat intelligence.
Trusted Automated Exchange of Intelligence Information: a protocol for sharing threat intelligence automatically.
A sector-based organisation through which members share threat information.
A periodically produced, digitally signed summary of log file hashes, used to prove logs haven’t changed.
Writing untrusted input to logs without escaping it, so crafted text can forge or corrupt entries (CWE-117).
Monitoring sequence numbers, heartbeats and volumes to find events lost between source and store.
A difference between system clocks that distorts timelines, prevented by synchronised time and timestamps in UTC.
A verified copy of evidence used for analysis, so the original stays unaltered.
Removing a value from data entirely, as is done for secrets.
Encryption that keeps the format of the original value, such as a 16-digit number.
Replacing exact values with ranges or categories, such as network ranges or age bands.
A protected store that maps tokens back to original values, controlled separately from the people who analyse tokens.
Masking sensitive data in the gateway, instrumentation or collector, before it is stored or forwarded.
A classifier or model-based judge that scores AI inputs and outputs as they happen.
A shift in the distribution of input embeddings away from a baseline, suggesting users are asking about different things.
A reversible, automated response to a high-risk detection, such as throttling a key or pausing an agent.
A unique string planted in a system prompt, document or record, whose appearance elsewhere reveals leakage or unauthorised access.
A decoy credential, record or document with no legitimate use, so any use or retrieval triggers an alert.
Checking retrieved documents and tool results for instructions addressed to the model before it processes them.
Disguising malicious input with encodings, translations, unusual characters or formatting to evade detection.
Use of one identity from locations too far apart to be reached in the time between them.
The approved tools, data and actions for an agent, recorded at approval and used as a baseline for detecting misuse.
The difference between the permissions an identity holds and those it actually uses; a large gap indicates excess privilege.
Secret scanning that confirms whether a detected credential is live, so real exposures are prioritised.
Issuing a new credential and revoking the old one, done immediately when a secret is exposed.
An agent reading sensitive data and then sending data to an external destination: a strong exfiltration signal.
An attempt by code-executing AI to start processes, reach the network or access files outside its sandbox’s permitted set.
Periodic re-verification that a loaded model, configuration or index still matches its approved hash or signature.
Cryptographically signing model files, for example with Sigstore-based OpenSSF model signing, so their origin and integrity can be verified.
A point-in-time copy of a vector index and its source records, used for evidence and clean restoration.
A sudden change in which documents are returned for common queries, which can indicate knowledge base poisoning.
Assessing alerts to decide their validity, severity and next steps.
Automatically closing alerts in narrowly defined, low-risk categories, with sampling to check accuracy.
Proactive, hypothesis-driven searching for attacker activity that existing detections have missed.
A threat hunting framework whose name stands for Prepare, Execute, Act with Knowledge.
Targeted Hunting integrating Threat Intelligence: a hunting methodology developed in the Dutch financial sector.
Designing, testing, deploying and tuning detection rules and analytics as a disciplined, versioned practice.
An AI tool that lets analysts ask questions in plain language, returning queries, summaries and evidence.
Instructions planted in attacker-controlled log fields, such as file names, aimed at AI assistants that read the logs.
A record of known weaknesses in AI models and components, with affected assets, evidence, severity, owner, treatment and status.
A record of where AI assets can be reached and by whom, used with the vulnerability register to judge urgency.
The public catalogue of uniquely identified software vulnerabilities.
Open Source Vulnerabilities: a database and schema for vulnerabilities in open-source packages.
An open knowledge base of AI failure modes and vulnerabilities.
A weakness in model quality, such as hallucination, that isn’t a security vulnerability unless an attacker can reliably exploit it.
The Common Vulnerability Scoring System, with base, threat, environmental and supplemental metric groups.
Exploit Prediction Scoring System: the estimated probability that a vulnerability will be exploited in the next 30 days.
CISA’s list of vulnerabilities with evidence of active exploitation.
Stakeholder-Specific Vulnerability Categorization: a decision tree leading to track, track*, attend or act.
The OWASP AI Vulnerability Scoring System: an emerging scoring approach focused first on agentic AI risks.
A vulnerability’s urgency once exposure, exploitation, data, privileges, existing controls and consequence are considered.
An assessment of the consequences of disruption to business processes, used to rank how critical systems are.
A control, such as a gateway rule, that blocks exploitation of a flaw while the real fix is prepared.
An alternative control that meets the intent and rigour of a requirement that can’t be applied directly.
A model that is out of support, or can’t easily be patched or replaced, but remains in use.
A formally approved deviation from a requirement, with compensating controls, a risk owner and an expiry date.
A limit on who may use a system, with what data, for which tasks and for how long.
A chain of weaknesses an attacker could link, such as an exposed endpoint, an over-privileged identity and sensitive data.
Automated tests that confirm key controls are operating, not just designed.
A metric of how well a programme performs, such as mean time to remediate.
The average time from discovering a finding to verifying its fix, tracked by priority.
A measure of AI security posture, such as coverage, hygiene, exposure or remediation, trended against targets.
A shared set of AI incident categories, such as prompt injection, jailbreaking, poisoning, model theft, leakage and agent misuse, used to triage consistently.
Input that makes a model follow instructions other than its intended ones: direct when typed by the user, indirect when hidden in content the model reads.
A form of prompt injection that gets a model to ignore its safety rules and produce content it should refuse.
Stealing a model’s weights, or copying its behaviour through systematic querying (model extraction).
An agent’s tools and permissions used to cause harm, through manipulation, error or a stolen identity.
A rating combining impact, spread and persistence that drives escalation and containment.
Harm that continues until it is cleaned up, such as a poisoned model, corrupted agent memory or a tainted index.
The notice of a significant incident that essential and important entities must send within 24 hours under NIS2.
Under the GDPR, a security breach leading to the accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration or unauthorised disclosure of, or access to, personal data.

An AI incident or malfunction leading to death or serious harm to health, serious and irreversible disruption of critical infrastructure, infringement of fundamental rights obligations, or serious harm to property or the environment.
Containment options ordered from least to most disruptive: tighten guardrails, throttle, restrict features, isolate, fall back or roll back, take offline.
Restricting and monitoring an attacker’s activity without alerting them, to preserve evidence.
A safe alternative, such as a simpler model, rule-based flow or manual process, used while the main AI system is unavailable.
A model and configuration confirmed, through lineage and testing, to predate an incident such as poisoning.
Freezing data ingestion, scheduled training and re-indexing, registry promotion and deployment during an incident.
A setting that prevents stored data, such as datasets, models and logs, from being deleted for a set period or until released.
Stopping an agent through controls outside the model: blocking new work, revoking credentials, holding pending actions and ending sessions.
An action that reverses the effect of an earlier one, such as a refund or record restore, used to undo agent actions.
Collecting the most fragile evidence first, such as runtime memory before logs and stored files.
A case record of every preserved item, with its source, collector, time, hash, storage location and legal hold status.
Information that exists only while a system runs, such as agent memory, session context, caches and queues.
The stages of an attack on an AI system, from reconnaissance and access through execution and persistence to exfiltration or impact.
The step in an agent trace where its plan diverged from the user’s intent, usually just after untrusted content entered its context.
The document, web page, email or tool result that delivered injected instructions to a model.
Hashing and comparing model files against approved versions to detect and locate tampering.
Comparing dataset versions to find records that were added, removed or altered.
Estimating which training examples most affected a particular model output; useful but approximate.
Searching for hidden inputs that make a model change its output unusually, as a backdoor would.
A single, UTC-normalised sequence of events merged from every relevant source in an investigation.
A structured method for finding the underlying technical and process causes of an incident, so it can’t recur.
The immediate cause of an incident, as opposed to the root causes that allowed it.
An RCA technique that asks "why?" repeatedly until it reaches a cause that, if fixed, prevents recurrence.
An RCA diagram that groups possible causes by category, such as data, model, people, process, technology and suppliers.
Reviewing incidents with a focus on systems and controls rather than individual blame, so people share what really happened.
A confidence-based judgement about who carried out an attack, drawn from infrastructure, techniques, artefacts and intelligence.
An intrusion analysis model linking adversary, capability, infrastructure and victim.
How an attacker operates; harder to change than infrastructure, so useful for attribution.
Evidence deliberately planted to make an attack look like the work of someone else.
Accessing an attacker’s systems in retaliation; unlawful in most jurisdictions.
Identifying, quarantining and removing poisoned or malicious records, then rebuilding a clean, hashed dataset version.
A saved model state that lineage shows was produced before the poisoned data was used.
A model fine-tuned or distilled from another, which can inherit its backdoors or poisoning.
Testing that a fixed or updated AI system still meets safety, security, quality and fairness criteria, and that the original attack now fails.
The attack inputs from an incident, plus variants, kept permanently in regression testing.
The evidence and sign-offs required before a system returns to production after an incident.
A model refusing legitimate requests, often after safety controls are tightened too far.
The maximum acceptable time to restore a service or component after disruption.
The maximum acceptable amount of data or change that can be lost, measured back from the disruption.
The longest a business process can be disrupted before the impact becomes unacceptable.
Redeploying a previous signed, approved model version from the registry.
Restoring an index from a clean snapshot, or rebuilding it from verified sources, then validating retrieval.
Test queries with known correct results, used to validate retrieval after an index is restored or changed.
A mechanism that trips automatically on safety, security, cost or reliability thresholds and diverts traffic to a fallback.
A circuit breaker state that lets limited trial traffic through after a cool-down, to test whether it is safe to close.
A defined condition a system moves to when stopped, including what happens to queued and in-flight work.
Planning so critical processes continue, or recover quickly, after disruption; set out in ISO 22301.
A record of the providers, compute, data, tools, identity and safety services an AI service relies on, with owners and fallbacks.
Running a reduced but safe service, such as a simpler model or rules, while full capability is unavailable.
Switching to a pre-tested alternative model or provider when the primary one is unavailable.
A structured, blameless review of an incident that produces owned, dated and verified improvement actions.
An internal catalogue of attacker techniques observed against the organisation, linked to detections, mitigations and tests.
Labels (CLEAR, GREEN, AMBER, AMBER+STRICT, RED) that tell recipients how widely they may share information.
The time from detecting an incident to stopping further harm.
Retiring an AI system completely: stopping traffic, revoking access, archiving or destroying artefacts and data, verifying sanitisation and updating records.
Unlearning methods, such as retraining only the affected data shards, that guarantee the data’s influence is removed.
A regulatory remedy requiring deletion of models and algorithms built with improperly obtained data.
Permanently retiring a model, its derived models and associated data, often as remediation for unfixable or unlawful risk.
Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis: a seven-stage, risk-centric threat modelling method linked to business objectives.
A privacy threat modelling method covering linking, identifying, non-repudiation, detecting, data disclosure, unawareness and non-compliance.
A diagram that breaks an attacker’s goal into the alternative steps and sub-goals that could achieve it.
In MAESTRO, a threat that starts in one layer of an agentic system and causes harm in another, such as poisoned memory hijacking a tool.
A catalogue of known threats and techniques, such as MITRE ATLAS or the OWASP lists, used to drive threat identification.
Describing a system and its threats in versioned, machine-readable files, using tools such as OWASP Threat Dragon, pytm or Threagile.
An attack that makes a model produce outputs or take actions the attacker chooses.
Bypassing a generative model’s safety controls to obtain harmful output; one of NIST’s attacker goals.
An attack by someone who knows the model’s architecture and weights.
An attack that uses only the model’s inputs and outputs.
Risk from people with legitimate access, whether malicious, negligent or compromised.
An agent, tool, server or bot that acts against an organisation’s interests, whoever controls it.
Crafting inputs at inference time so that a deployed model produces wrong outputs.
An input deliberately perturbed, often imperceptibly, to make a model err.
An adversarial input developed against a proxy model and then used against a different target model.
Planting crafted documents in a RAG knowledge base to steer answers to targeted questions.
Writing content so that it ranks first for chosen queries in a retrieval system.
Planting sources that lend false authority to an AI system’s answers.
Injected content or manipulation that redirects what an agent is trying to achieve (OWASP ASI01).
Corrupting an agent’s persistent memory or shared context so planted instructions affect later work (OWASP ASI06).
An error or compromise in one agent or component that spreads through others (OWASP ASI08).
People over-trusting agents, or agents manipulating people, leading to harmful approvals (OWASP ASI09).
An agent acting outside its intended purpose or control (OWASP ASI10).
Text placed in an image that a multimodal model reads and follows as an instruction.
Synthetic audio, images or video that convincingly imitate a real person.
Filling requests to the maximum input length to drive up cost and latency.
Prompts designed to force very long, costly outputs.
An input crafted to maximise a model’s computation, energy use and latency.
Separate queues or capacity for critical services or tenants, so abuse of one can’t starve the others.
The largest change an attacker may make to an input in an evasion attack, measured with a norm such as L∞ or L2.
A one-step evasion attack that moves every input value by ε in the direction of the sign of the loss gradient.
An iterative evasion attack that takes many small gradient steps, projecting back into the perturbation budget after each.
An optimisation-based evasion attack that searches for the smallest perturbation that causes misclassification.
An ensemble of parameter-free attacks used as a reliable benchmark for adversarial robustness.
A defence effect that breaks gradient-based attacks without making the model robust; adaptive attacks get around it.
An attack designed with full knowledge of a specific defence; the standard for credible robustness claims.
A black-box evasion attack that estimates gradients from how a model’s confidence scores change.
A black-box evasion attack that needs only the predicted labels, walking along the decision boundary.
A single perturbation that causes a model to misclassify most inputs it is added to.
A model an attacker trains on similar data with known members, to learn what training-set membership looks like.
A strong membership inference attack that compares a record’s loss under models trained with and without it.
The stages of building and running AI (plan and design, data, build and train, evaluate, release, operate and retire), each with security activities.
Practices and tooling for building, deploying and operating machine learning models reliably, such as versioning, pipelines, registries and monitoring.
MLOps adapted for applications built on large language models, adding prompt management, evaluation harnesses, guardrails, RAG pipelines and provider version management.
NIST’s set of secure development practices (SP 800-218), with a profile for generative AI in SP 800-218A.

t: UK AI Cyber Security Code of Practice
d: UK government principles (2025) for securing AI across design, development, deployment, maintenance and end of life.
An ETSI technical specification (2025) setting baseline cyber security requirements for AI models and systems.
The international standard for AI system life cycle processes.
A pipeline step that blocks release unless safety, security and quality evaluations meet agreed thresholds.
Versioning, reviewing, testing and deploying prompt templates as controlled artefacts.
An isolated environment for experiments, using synthetic or masked data and no production credentials.
Moving a registered, approved model version from one environment to the next through the pipeline.
A connection to a provider’s service over a private network path rather than the public internet.
A record pinning every behaviour-changing component of an AI release: model, data, prompts, index, guardrails, tools and evaluation results.
A pre-approved, low-risk change following an agreed pattern, such as a scheduled index refresh from approved sources.
