A change assessed and approved individually according to risk, such as a new model or tool.
Running a candidate and the current version on the same test suites to expose differences before release.
Running a new version on real inputs without showing its outputs or allowing side effects, to compare behaviour safely.
Splitting traffic between versions to compare their real-world outcomes.
A switch that turns a capability on or off for chosen users or groups without redeploying.
Releasing to progressively wider groups, such as staff, then pilot customers, then everyone.
A pre-agreed threshold on safety, quality, operational or business signals that reverts a rollout automatically.
Designing changes, such as data or schema migrations, so that rolling back doesn’t break or corrupt the system.
Risk from your vendors’ own suppliers, such as the model providers an AI vendor sends your data to.
AI functionality added to a product you already use, sometimes enabled by default, which can change data flows without a new contract.

An independent auditor’s report on a service organisation’s controls against the AICPA Trust Services Criteria. Type I covers design at a point in time; Type II also covers operating effectiveness over a period.
Controls a SOC report assumes the customer operates. If the customer doesn’t, the assurance doesn’t fully apply.
Excluding a subservice organisation’s controls from a SOC report, so separate evidence is needed for that supplier.
A statement by vendor management covering the gap between a SOC report’s period end and the present. It isn’t audited.
The 2025 standard setting extra requirements for bodies that audit and certify AI management systems against ISO/IEC 42001.
A vendor portal that publishes security and compliance documents, often behind a non-disclosure agreement.
A short statement that a test or audit took place. It doesn’t replace the report’s scope, findings and remediation status.
A custom model licence allowing broad use under conditions, such as an acceptable use policy, naming rules or a user threshold.
A licence, such as OpenRAIL-M, that prohibits specified uses and requires the restrictions to be passed on to recipients.
The Open Source Initiative’s 2024 definition, requiring access to model weights, code and detailed information about training data.
EU AI Act rules (Article 25) under which a party that rebrands, substantially modifies or repurposes a high-risk system becomes its provider.
US federal guidance (April 2025) on acquiring AI, covering IP rights, portability and a ban on vendors training on non-public agency data without consent.
A model’s lineage: its ancestors, the derivation steps between them, the data used and the producers involved.
Signing an approved third-party artefact with your organisation’s own identity, so deployment policy needs to trust only one internal signer.
An MLCommons machine-readable metadata format for machine learning datasets, with fields for responsible AI information.
An inventory of a system’s physical components, such as processors, accelerators and firmware.
Machine-readable statements of whether a product is affected by a vulnerability: affected, not affected (with a justification), fixed or under investigation.
A 2025 Rowhammer attack on GPU memory, showing that bit flips could sharply degrade model accuracy when error correction was disabled.
G7 guidance (2026) listing seven clusters of information an AI bill of materials should contain, from metadata to key performance indicators.
A mismatch between a deployed system and its AIBOM, for example after a manual hotfix that bypassed the pipeline.
Emulating adversaries, and users who stumble into harm, to find how an AI system fails, usually in repeated break-fix cycles.
A signed agreement setting a test’s authority, scope, objectives, methods, limits, stop rules, timing and reporting.
A pre-agreed condition, such as real data appearing, that halts testing and triggers escalation.
A planned test naming an actor, an entry point, a technique class, a target and the evidence that proves success.
A map of technique classes against system components, showing what has and hasn’t been tested.
Testing with no internal knowledge of the system.
Testing with partial internal knowledge, such as the architecture and system prompts.
Testing with full access, including code, configuration and sometimes model weights.
A harmless tool that only records that it was called, used to prove that an agent followed injected instructions.
A test of whether injected instructions survive into later sessions or other users’ sessions.
An attack spread across several conversation turns, building up gradually to evade safeguards.
Attackers and defenders working together during testing, so that detections and controls improve as findings emerge.
Repeated rounds of testing, mitigation and retesting that raise attackers’ costs over time.
Using attacker models, scorers and orchestration to generate and evaluate adversarial tests at scale.
A model used to generate and refine adversarial inputs against a target system.
A classifier, rule or model that judges whether a response shows a successful attack.
Microsoft’s open-source Python Risk Identification Tool for automated red teaming of generative AI.
NVIDIA’s open-source scanner that probes language models for known weaknesses.
The UK AI Security Institute’s open-source framework for building and running AI evaluations.
An agent that combines access to private data, exposure to untrusted content and the ability to communicate externally.
OWASP’s 2025 blueprint for red teaming generative AI across model, implementation, infrastructure and runtime.

t: CSA Agentic AI Red Teaming Guide
d: 2025 guidance from the Cloud Security Alliance and OWASP AI Exchange setting out twelve threat categories for testing AI agents.
An automated system that finds and patches software vulnerabilities, such as those in DARPA’s AI Cyber Challenge.
A programme that rewards external researchers for reporting vulnerabilities within agreed rules.
A jailbreak root cause in which a model’s drive to be helpful and follow instructions is set against its safety training.
A jailbreak root cause in which a model’s abilities extend to inputs, such as encodings or rare languages, that its safety training didn’t cover.
Filling a long context window with many fabricated dialogues in which an assistant complies, so that the model follows the pattern.
A jailbreak that moves towards a refused goal in small conversational steps, each harmless alone; Crescendo is a published example.
An attack that uses model gradients to search for an adversarial suffix token by token; its suffixes can transfer to other models.
Sampling many random variations of a request until one gets through; success keeps rising with the number of attempts.
Splitting a request into fragments that are harmless separately and asking the model to combine them.
The share of legitimate requests that a model or guardrail wrongly refuses or blocks.
An open benchmark and leaderboard for evaluating jailbreak attacks and defences on language models.
Validating, deduplicating, rating and prioritising assessment findings so the most important are fixed first.
How much skill, access and effort an attacker needs to use a weakness.
How reliably a finding recurs, reported as a success rate over repeated attempts with versions and settings recorded.
Whether monitoring would notice a weakness being exploited.
Grouping variants that share a root cause into a single finding, with the variants kept as evidence.
A limit on access to data, actions or systems; crossing one without authorisation is what makes a finding a vulnerability.
A 2025 zero-click vulnerability (CVE-2025-32711) in Microsoft 365 Copilot, in which injected content could make the assistant leak internal data.
A catalogue of weakness types, including CWE-1427 for unneutralised LLM prompt input and CWE-1426 for unvalidated generative AI output.
Linking each finding to relevant entries in frameworks such as MITRE ATLAS, the OWASP Top 10s and CWE.
Using mapped findings and test records to show which risk categories were tested, and which were not.
The versions, settings, inputs, expected and observed results, rates and evidence needed to repeat a finding.
The shortest input and fewest steps that still reproduce a finding.
Leading a report or briefing with the decision needed and its impact.
A short, plain-language overview of the top risks, the decisions needed and the options.
A control that held during testing, reported alongside the findings.
Reporting a flaw privately to the vendor, allowing time for a fix before publication.
The international standard for vulnerability disclosure.
The international standard for vendors’ vulnerability handling processes.
Google’s 2025 bug bounty for AI products, rewarding security impacts such as rogue actions and data exfiltration rather than content issues.
A control aimed at the root cause of a specific attack class, such as data validation for poisoning.
Adding attack examples, with correct labels or safe responses, to training so a model learns to resist them.
Transforming inputs before inference, for example by normalising or denoising them, to weaken evasion attacks.
A mathematical guarantee that a model’s output won’t change for any input within a defined distance of the original.
An agent design that can trigger actions but never reads their outputs, so tool results can’t steer it.
Processing each untrusted item in an isolated worker, and combining only constrained results.
A privileged model writes a program in a restricted language, so the flow of untrusted data can be tracked and checked.
Removing content that later steps don’t need, so it can’t influence them.
Anthropic’s 2025 input and output classifiers, trained on synthetic data generated from a set of principles, to block jailbreaks.
Google’s watermarking technology for AI-generated text, images, audio and video.
A temporary measure, such as disabling a tool, that contains a risk while the full fix is built.
A mitigation that removes a large amount of risk for little effort.
Modify, avoid, share or retain a risk, as set out in risk standards such as ISO/IEC 27005.
Attack variants kept out of any tuning, so they remain a fair test of whether a fix generalises.
A mitigation that blocks the exact reported input but not the underlying weakness.
A loss of quality or helpfulness caused by a change, such as a new safety control.
Change in residual risk over time, as models, tools and attack techniques change.
Automated adversarial testing rerun on a timer against a production-equivalent system.
Resistance shown by surviving the strongest known attacks; a new attack may still break it.
A certified defence that classifies many noisy copies of an input and returns the majority label with a certified L2 radius, or abstains.
An adversarial training method that makes the trade-off between clean accuracy and robustness explicit and tunable.
A failure of fast, single-step adversarial training in which robustness to iterative attacks suddenly collapses.
The decline in robust test accuracy that can follow its peak during adversarial training; early stopping helps.
A separate classifier that screens a model’s inputs or outputs against a safety or security policy.
Meta’s open-weight safety classifiers that label prompts and responses against a hazard taxonomy.
An Azure AI Content Safety feature that detects attacks in user prompts and in documents a model processes.
NVIDIA’s open-source toolkit for programmable rails on a model’s inputs, dialogue, retrieval and outputs, written in Colang.
A defence that flags inputs whose text is statistically unnatural, such as machine-optimised adversarial suffixes.
Allowing activity through when a security control is unavailable, which attackers can exploit by overloading the control.
An incorrect answer option designed to look plausible, often by being partly true or the right action at the wrong time.
A planned progress point during the exam, such as reaching question 40 at about 45 minutes.
A question marked to revisit if time allows, after choosing a best answer for it.
A full-length, timed practice exam weighted like the real one, used to test readiness and find weak domains.
